cards.title: Future wars
cards.author: Aizaz Ahmad Chaudhry
cards.why: This is essential for understanding the shift in global power dynamics, military technology, and the breakdown of the UN-led international order.
cards.summary: Modern warfare has evolved beyond traditional mechanised combat into a complex hybrid model involving cyberattacks, economic coercion, and psychological manipulation. Lethal technologies, including autonomous weapons, precision missiles, and armed drones, have replaced old battlefield strategies. These advancements allow for rapid, long-range strikes but lack the nuanced understanding of human context.
key_facts: Wars today use autonomous weapons guided by specialised semiconductors, microchips, and sensors.
Advanced drones and robotic systems are now used for intelligence gathering and targeted strikes.
Autonomous systems currently lack the capability to comprehend the context of a conflict.
Missiles guided by infrared sensors and satellite communication have replaced many conventional engagement tactics.

vocab.meaning: Combining different types of elements or methods.
The practice of persuading someone to do something by using force or threats.

text: THE four-day military confrontation between India and Pakistan last year and the US-Iran war this year have revealed how today’s wars have become far more complex than the conventional conflicts humanity has experienced over millennia. The days of massed soldiery, mechanised armour, and standardised formations are over. Today’s wars are hybrid and employ every instrument of power a state can muster.
These wars involve cyberattacks, economic coercion, psychological manipulation through electronic and social media, and cultural invasions.

Critically, today’s wars employ lethal technologies, which have left traditional battlefield concepts behind. These autonomous weapons are guided by specialised semiconductors, microchips, and sensors.

The changing nature of war has coincided with the sharp descent of the world order into disarray. Wars and armed conflicts between and within states have broken out in various parts of the world. The pledge that all states had made to the UN Charter to respect each other’s sovereignty and territorial integrity is no longer being honoured.

Two distinguishing features of today’s warfare are advanced missiles and armed drones, which have transformed the nature of war by enabling high-precision, long-range, and rapid response capabilities.

In last year’s India-Pakistan war, Pakistan used missiles to down several Indian aircraft flying well beyond visual range. In the US-Iran war this year, both sides relied mostly on missiles guided by infrared sensors and satellite communication rather than conventional confrontation.
Autonomous weapons lack the capability to understand the context.

Advanced robotic systems are being employed for intelligence, surveillance, and even targeted strikes. Drones and robotic dogs can provide real-time data, improve combat efficiency, and operate for high-risk functions such as clearance of mines or locating captured personnel. Unarmed aerial vehicles provide real-time intelligence, and are equipped with AI-driven capabilities to analyse data. Targets can be independently tracked and even struck by loitering munitions or suicide drones. Transporting supplies and ammunition entails no life losses thanks to unarmed ground vehicles. Drone swarms can now be trained to carry out coordinated attacks. It’s only a matter of time before humanoid robots are deployed for military roles.

The spectrum of modern wars employs other technologies as well, such as quantum computing, which solves complex problems faster than classical computers. It ensures unhackable and secure data transmission during conflict situations. Next-generation structural battery composites can store energy for longer periods.

Future wars will move further away from face-to-face engagement or human-controlled systems. Intelligent autonomous systems will be central to making decisions, often without human intervention. However, this raises some serious ethical questions.

Autonomous weapons lack the capability to understand the context or apply compassion. There is greater likelihood of violating the laws of war and committing war crimes without assigning accountability. Further, the speed and agility of these technologies could cause conflicts to spiral out of control.

These technologies will also be used to break an adversary’s morale by targeting its economic assets or supply chains. During the Iran war, for instance, President Trump threatened to destroy Iran’s power grid and bridges, even its civilisation.

The kind of technologies a nation possesses will now determine the extent of damage that a future war would impose on an adversary’s policy options. The ability of a nation to acquire and em­­ploy modern technologies is thus critical to both wag­-ing future wars and surviving them.

What makes future wars more frequent and unaccountable is the evolving global ecosystem, where use of force has emerged as the primary arbiter of international relations. Major powers have no qualms about using force illegally, unilaterally, and disproportionately to overpower adversaries.

In such an uncertain environment, middle and small powers are looking for ways to fend for themselves and make alliances with like-minded countries. This has nudged countries to focus more on R&D for developing not only war-related technologies but also their own digital and satellite-based communication links. That requires a stronger economy, credible information instruments, and creative narrative-building to deter aggression.

Diplomatic tools must be geared up to avert such complex multidomain future wars. The world needs a new global compact of indivisible security, akin to the UN Charter, to bind states into mutual respect for each other’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. This is the only way to avert the devastating wars of the future.
The writer is Chairman Sanober Institute and former foreign secretary of Pakistan.
Published in Dawn, November 22nd, 2026

cards.title: Legislative scrutiny
cards.author: Ahmed Bilal Mehboob
cards.why: It provides critical insight into the administrative cost, structure, and functional challenges of Pakistan's parliamentary oversight system.
cards.summary: Pakistan’s legislative infrastructure consists of over 200 parliamentary committees across national and provincial houses. While members receive significant financial benefits and administrative support, these committees often function during recess periods. This contrasts with the British model where committees only meet during plenary sessions and the Indian model which utilizes joint committees to improve efficiency.
key_facts: There are 35 parliamentary committees in the National Assembly and 45 in the Senate.
Provincial assembly committees count 45 in Punjab, 34 in Sindh, 38 in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, and 15 in Balochistan.
Committee chairs are provided with two personal staffers and a chauffeur-driven official car.
Pakistan's committee system differs from the British model by meeting during legislative recess, increasing travel and allowance costs.

vocab.meaning: A session attended by all members of a legislative body.
A period when the proceedings of a parliament are temporarily suspended.

text: PAKISTAN’S parliament and the provincial assemblies have an elaborate infrastructure of parliamentary oversight and scrutiny of the executive. There are more than 200 parliamentary committees in the six houses, including 35 in the National Assembly, 45 in the Senate, 45 in the provincial assembly of Punjab, 34 in Sindh, 38 in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and 15 in Balochistan.

Each committee comprises 20 to 30 members varying from house to house. These members elect a committee chair in their first meeting; the chair is entitled to two personal staffers, a chauffeur-driven and fully maintained official car and an exclusive office. The committee members and the chair are entitled to travel and daily allowances for the days of the meeting and two days before and after the meeting. All this is paid for from the taxpayers’ pocket and is fully justified in view of the work assigned to these committees. Unlike the British parliamentary committees, which meet only during the plenary sessions of parliament and therefore do not incur any extra travel or daily allowance cost, parliamentary committees in Pakistan mostly meet when the legislature is in recess and hence, extra travel and daily allowances are to be paid separately.

The Indian parliament has adopted another measure and constituted joint committees of the Lok Sabha (equivalent to our National Assembly) and the Rajya Sabha (like Pakistan’s Senate), which not only speeds up scrutiny in the committees, but results in some savings as well. In Pakistan, we have independent and separate committees both for the National Assembly and the Senate. Although the Indian joint committees system is efficient, it deprives parliament of a double layer of scrutiny which is available in Pakistan.
The problem arises when important bills are summarily processed within days or even hours.

In all systems of governance, whether presidential like the US, parliamentary like the UK and Pakistan, the parliaments — whatever name these are known as — rely on the committees to do most of the substantive work, especially the oversight of the executive, which primarily includes scrutiny of legislation. In any work which requires detailed scrutiny like the annual budget, a constitutional amendment, ordinary legislation or, as in the case of the US, confirmation of senior appointees in the executive and judiciary, committees play a pivotal role. It is not practical to do such work in plenary.

Rules of almost all the legislatures in Pakistan provide that each legislation, after it is introduced in the plenary, will be referred to the relevant committee for detailed deliberations and scrutiny. In extraordinary circumstances, the plenary has the authority to suspend the rule and consider the legislation in the plenary without referring it to the committee concerned. One of the criteria by which the quality of democracy and effectiveness of legislative oversight in a country is assessed is the percentage of legislation which is not referred to the committees; the higher the percentage, the less democratic and effective the country and the legislature are considered. An associated criterion is the time taken and the number of meetings held to scrutinise the legislation in a committee. If legislation is referred to a committee to fulfil a formality and the committee returns it to the plenary in a day or two, it reflects very negatively on the democratic credentials of the parliament.

As far as the number of bills passed by the legislatures is concerned, Pakistan has a reasonably good record. In the National Assembly, an average of 50 bills have been passed per year during the past four assemblies. The problem arises when the bills, especially the most important ones like constitutional amendments, are summarily processed within a couple of days, and sometimes within hours. For example, a record 279 bills were passed during the previous 15th National Assembly (2018-2023), which is the highest compared to the previous three assemblies starting from 2002.

Although legislative activity had increased, the way these bills were passed without debate and scrutiny of the committees was widely criticised by legislators, media and political commentators. The coalition government passed 73 bills in the last session alone within 21 days. Almost half the bills (36) were not referred to the standing committees concerned and rushed through the plenary without a meaningful debate.

The current 16th National Assembly has so far passed 162 bills in its 32 months of existence. The National Assembly data shown on its official website does not indicate the statistics about the bills referred to the committees or otherwise. Transparency demands that this particular information should be available to citizens and media. In the absence of such data, time-consuming research needs to be undertaken bill by bill to know the extent to which the standing committees were involved in the legislative process.

According to analysis carried out by Pildat, 39 per cent of the bills passed by the current assembly so far were not referred to the committees and instead, the rules were suspended to pass the bill in the plenary directly. This translates to 48 (38pc) government bills and 15 (42pc) private members’ bills. This, by no means, is a good record.

The situation becomes even more disappointing when we see that such important legislation such as the 26th and 27th Constitutional Amendments — which have had far-reaching impact on state institutions like the judiciary and the armed forces — are passed within a couple of days. The 26th Amendment was introduced in the Senate on Oct 20, 2024 and was passed the same day. The National Assembly passed it the next day and the president gave his assent later in the day. It was notified in the Gazette later in the evening. Such important legislation was wrapped up in two days. The 27th Amendment was also passed with the same hurry.
Laws decide the fate of a nation for a long time. It is about time our legislative leadership gave more time to the committees and the plenary to improve the quality of legislation.
The writer is president of Pakistan-based think tank, Pildat.

cards.title: Reforming Karachi’s governance
cards.author: Dr Noman Ahmed
cards.why: It highlights the administrative and structural crises facing Pakistan's largest city, which is vital for the Governance paper.
cards.summary: Governance in Karachi faces a paradox between superficial beautification projects and systemic failure in essential urban services. Fragmentation of roles and budgetary issues has severely hampered infrastructure development compared to the past when the Karachi Development Authority operated with greater autonomy. Effective reform requires moving beyond political disputes to restore functional capacity in planning and engineering.
key_facts: Karachi residents frequently report issues with water supply, waste management, transport, and air quality.
Current municipal governance suffers from fragmented roles and unclear budgetary allocations.
The Karachi Development Authority historically maintained infrastructure standards through a team of professional technocrats and engineers.
Local government entities have struggled with political rucksacks and low ground-level engagement with the public.

vocab.meaning: A situation that seems contradictory or impossible.
The process of breaking something into small, separate parts.
Technical experts who are in charge of decision-making.

text: KARACHI’S governance appears to be in a serious paradox. On one hand, one finds political leaders of various ranks cutting ribbons and unveiling plaques around pedestrianised food streets and making promises for more such amenities. On the other hand, a major regional financial institution is expressing its frustration with the alleged inability of the government for slow progress on a major transportation project. The ordinary resident of Karachi is ever critical of the poor service levels in respect to water supply, sewerage, waste management, disruptions in transport corridors, rising road accidents, declining air quality and many other problems.

It is also disappointing to note that in many neighbourhoods, the local government entities have also fared poorly. While the news of ruckus in the municipal halls between rival political factions does reach the common man through media reports, the presence on the ground and engagement of municipal councillors and office-bearers of other ranks is conspicuous by its absence. There are several points that need to be reviewed to bring about real reform.

In the present form, there is fragmentation in roles, responsibilities and budgetary allocations for routine affairs. Take infrastructure development as an example. In the past, this task was largely performed by the Karachi Development Authority (KDA). Bridges, culverts, siphons, flyovers, arterial roads, parks, playgrounds, pedestrian bridges and a range of other components of infrastructure were planned, designed and developed either through departmental undertaking or through consultancy and contractual arrangement. As the authority was manned by capable technocrats and dedicated engineers and staff, the quality of works was satisfactory. Many of these facilities still continue to serve, with minor repairs and adjustments.
A Karachi-level steering committee should be formed comprising the heads of all civic bodies functioning under the Sindh government.

It was assumed that with the expansion of the city, increase in population and other complexities, new entities were needed to perform similar functions. Two new development authorities were created for Lyari and Malir. Similar functions were assigned to them. But the overall performance, quality of human resource, and capability to perform those functions stipulated in their respective laws leaves much to be desired. We now have multiple authorities, entities and corporations for overlapping tasks. We have separate authorities and entities for managing mass transit, waste management, katchi abadis, master planning, water supply and sewerage, and construction of bus rapid transit (BRT). An ordinary resident is directly or indirectly affected by the performance of these entities or lack thereof. Citizens are unsure whom to contact in respect of any specific grievance. Additionally, the three-tier municipal system with a metropolitan corporation, town municipal corporations and union committees adds further to this confusion. If an excavator comes and digs the lane in front of houses without notice, the residents run from pillar to post to find out the real culprit. In an ideal situation, if these entities were responding to their assigned tasks and delivering services according to mandates, the situation may have been acceptable. But this is not what one observes.

The political leadership at the provincial and city level generally speaks in quantitative terms. Number of development schemes announced, ongoing and completed; inauguration ceremonies held; billions of rupees budgeted, processed and spent; and the geographical locations covered are some of the figures of speech in performance claims highlighted by politicians. But none of these helps the ordinary citizen in addressing the chronic issues this metropolis continues to suffer from.

There is an exponential rise in the city’s population due to migration. Poor law and order conditions in many parts of the country and loss of livelihood in several underdeveloped locations push people towards Karachi for survival. The bulk of this population needs basic urban services and low-skill employment opportunities to access a decent living. Urban housing is a perennial issue, especially for those who wish to start a new life.

Due to ultra-high prices of developer-built housing, overcrowding in the existing housing stock results. The extremely low number of large public buses makes a decent commute an uphill task. While BRTs are being planned and developed, they will only account for a fraction of total passenger trips generated daily in the city. Drinking water comes with a cost. Where piped water is available, its quality remains questionable.

Even in katchi abadis, people buy water from shops with unverified brand names and tariffs. There is a serious parking crisis in the southern and eastern commercial zones of the city. Vendors and hawkers along transport corridors are routinely evicted, though they sell merchandise at prices generally conducive to low-income households. But there are no designated spaces for hawkers and vendors’ markets. The city also suffers from absence of animal shelters and asylums. A sizable animal population suffers from cruelty. This must be addressed.

So, what can be done? There are several steps that can be taken almost instantly. A Karachi-level steering committee can be constituted comprising the heads of all the civic bodies functioning under the auspices of the provincial government. This committee must review the individual performance of each authority according to its legal mandate and suggest reforms where required.

The operational and financial details of planned, ongoing and completed projects must be put on a central digital dashboard, accessible to citizens. A complaint redressal system for service delivery agencies must be put in place. Some agencies do have complaint-registration windows, but the general response is very slow. A broad-based consultation must be carried out with the citizens of Karachi whenever any major development initiative or urban planning work is undertaken. Without the people’s input, development has no relevance.
The writer is an academic and researcher based in Karachi.
Published in Dawn, November 22nd, 2026
